assessment.nobel_worthiness: A discovery in the strict sense: the 2012 observation of a new boson at 125 GeV completed the Standard Model's electroweak sector and, through measured couplings, is now a precision probe of the mechanism of mass generation. The 2013 prize recognised the theory; the experimental discovery remains the natural complement.
assessment.attribution: The decisive experimental credit is institutional and collective. The supplied names are the founding-era leaders of ATLAS and CMS (Jenni, Della Negra, Virdee) and are a defensible but imperfect proxy for thousands of collaborators; the committee would also have to weigh the spokespersons at the time of discovery, and the Statutes' three-person limit makes this contested.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. Two independent experiments, large datasets and consistent coupling measurements back the interpretation; recognition is, if anything, overdue.
uncertainties: Whether a prize for founders/leaders rather than the discovery-year spokespersons or analysis conveners is fair; I rely on general knowledge, not verified detail.
The Standard Model Higgs may be only part of a richer scalar sector, but that does not affect the discovery itself.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: WMAP turned the CMB into a precision laboratory for cosmology: acoustic peaks, a flat geometry, a tightly measured cosmological-parameter set and early evidence for reionization, building the concordance LambdaCDM model. Its impact on theory (inflation, dark energy, dark matter) is large and clear.
assessment.attribution: Bennett as PI, Page as a leading instrument and experimental scientist, and Spergel as the lead on analysis and cosmological interpretation form a plausible three-way split, although the WMAP science team was large and others (e.g. Wilkinson, Hinshaw) have claims.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Confirmed and extended by Planck and ground-based CMB experiments; the results are stable. The COBE prize (2006) and the 2019 cosmology prize reduce, but do not eliminate, the room for another cosmology award.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views WMAP as a sufficiently distinct step beyond COBE, given that Planck has since superseded it.
Allocation among the larger WMAP team is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* are direct visual evidence for black holes and strong-field gravity, a discovery that speaks directly to my own field of black-hole physics. The experimental achievement (global mm-VLBI, calibration and imaging) is considerable and the result is widely appreciated.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow-imaging concept in 2000 and Doeleman led the technical realisation and the EHT collaboration; Zensus is a leading VLBI figure, but I would not put him among the decisive contributors. The collaboration is very large, which makes a fair three-person split hard.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature: M87* was observed in 2017 and imaged in 2019, Sgr A* in 2022, with consistent ring sizes. Polarisation and time-resolved follow-up are ongoing; the interpretation of the images is stable, though precision tests of GR remain modest.
uncertainties: Whether the imaging is a discovery or a spectacular demonstration of what was already expected.
Credit among the many contributors (e.g. instrument builders, algorithm developers) is hard to resolve.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, then its observation in HgTe quantum wells, opened the field of topological quantum matter, with a very large effect across condensed-matter physics, photonics and materials science.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the theoretical foundation; Molenkamp led the experimental realisation (with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as theorists of the HgTe proposal, and Moore, Balents, Roy, Fu and others on three-dimensional generalisation), so a three-person set leaves out some serious claims.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with multiple materials, ARPES and transport confirmations; the framework is stable. The 2016 prize on topological phases partly overlaps, which could count against it.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 Nobel Prize and unresolved credit for the HgTe proposal and three-dimensional topological insulators.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of the double pulsar PSR J0737-3039A/B gave a uniquely clean strong-field laboratory: multiple post-Keplerian parameters, a mass-ratio test independent of the gravity theory, and the best known tests of GR in the strong-field regime. It is a clear natural-world clue to gravity rather than a purely theoretical argument.
assessment.attribution: Burgay found the system, Lyne led the survey team and Kramer led the long-term timing and the GR tests; this is a defensible trio. Others in the discovery team (e.g. Possenti, Manchester, Camilo) could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: Mature after twenty years of timing, with agreement with GR at roughly the 0.01 percent level. Hulse and Taylor's 1993 prize and the 2017 gravitational-wave prize partly cover related ground, so novelty may be questioned.
uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the double pulsar as a step beyond the binary pulsar already honoured.
Weighting between discovery and later precision-timing work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2013 detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos and later source evidence (TXS 0506+056, the Galactic plane) opened neutrino astronomy at TeV-PeV energies, a new messenger and a discovery with concrete natural-world content.
assessment.attribution: Halzen is widely seen as the intellectual driver and IceCube's principal investigator; Spiering is a long-time leader of the project. Allocation versus other founders (e.g. Learned, Pak, Karle, Kowalski and the early AMANDA/DUMAND teams) is contested, and a very large collaboration is involved.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature, with an observation at high significance and increasing source associations; the source populations are still not understood, so interpretation remains evolving.
uncertainties: Whether the field is ready: sources of the diffuse flux are only partly identified.
Credit among founders, and the role of the large collaboration, is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene created the moire-materials field, with a rapid and broad scientific impact and a conceptually clean story.
assessment.attribution: The attribution is relatively clean: Bistritzer and MacDonald for the flat-band prediction and Jarillo-Herrero for the experimental discovery (with Cao and collaborators doing much of the experimental work). Others (e.g. Dean, Young, Santos and Peres, Lopes dos Santos) have claims.
assessment.maturity: Young: discovered in 2018 and confirmed by many groups, but the mechanism of superconductivity and the correlated phases is still debated, so a prize may be premature.
uncertainties: Premature recognition risk, given the open questions on the pairing mechanism.
Whether early student-led experimental contributions can be recognised under the three-person limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, achieve fractional uncertainties below 1e-18 and are changing time metrology, enabling relativistic geodesy and sensitive tests of fundamental constants and dark-sector physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori conceived the magic-wavelength lattice clock; Ye drove the strontium clock to record accuracy and the combination with frequency combs. This is a clean two-person attribution, although Hall and Hänsch (2005) have already been honoured for combs, and Ovsiannikov, Takamoto and others also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Mature and steadily confirmed by several laboratories, with a redefinition of the second under discussion; the timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: The 2012 and 2005 clock/comb prizes could reduce the appetite for a further metrology award.
Ye also appears in the thorium nuclear-clock entry; I only treat this one as a decisive entry.
